title: “SUSTAIN ME WITH RAISINS… FOR I AM SICK WITH LOVE”: THE PHYSICAL INTENSITY OF BIBLICAL DESIRE
paragraphs: “SUSTAIN ME WITH RAISINS… FOR I AM SICK WITH LOVE”: THE PHYSICAL INTENSITY OF BIBLICAL DESIRE

What if Scripture’s most startling picture of desire is not a warning against feeling deeply—but a revelation that God created human love with enough force to make the body tremble, the appetite disappear, and the heart ache… while still insisting that love must never be awakened outside its proper time?
There are verses in the Bible we read comfortably.
And then there are verses that almost make us look over our shoulder before reading them aloud.
Song of Songs 2:5 is one of those verses.
The woman does not merely say, “I love him.”
She does not say, “I think he is attractive.”
She does not offer us the sanitized vocabulary we sometimes prefer when discussing desire in church.

סַמְּכוּנִי בָּאֲשִׁישׁוֹת
רַפְּדוּנִי בַּתַּפּוּחִים
כִּי־חוֹלַת אַהֲבָה אָנִי
Samkhuni ba’ashishot, rapp’duni battappuchim, ki-cholat ahavah ani.
“Sustain me with raisin cakes, refresh me with apples, for I am faint with love.”
Or, more literally in its force:
And suddenly one of the Bible’s most beautiful love poems confronts something many Christians have spent years trying not to talk about:
The human body can participate in what the heart desires.
And Scripture is not embarrassed to tell us.
Because some people grew up believing that holiness meant becoming almost suspicious of being human.
Some were taught what not to do but were never taught what God actually created.
So they entered adulthood knowing how to feel guilty about desire without knowing how to understand it.
Then Song of Songs walks into the room.
And a woman saying she is practically overwhelmed by love.
Not smuggled into Scripture by someone who forgot Christians would eventually read it.
God permitted this astonishing celebration of covenantal human love to stand within Holy Scripture.

The woman has just described her beloved as an apple tree among the trees of the forest. She delights to sit beneath his shade. His fruit is sweet to her taste. He brings her into a place of feasting, and love is over her. Then comes the cry:
“His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me.”
Then Scripture does something extraordinarily important.
The next verse warns the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken or arouse love until the proper time.
Because the Bible does not solve the intensity of desire by declaring desire evil.
Biblical holiness is not the murder of desire.
It is the consecration of desire.
Fire inside a fireplace can warm a home.
Fire unleashed across the living room can destroy it.
The problem is not that fire possesses heat.
The question is where the fire belongs.
And perhaps someone reading this has spent years hating the fire simply because nobody taught you the fireplace.
You felt attraction and immediately felt dirty.
You wanted to be wanted and immediately felt ashamed.
You longed to be held, known, chosen, pursued, cherished—and wondered whether serious Christians were supposed to outgrow such things.
Song of Songs refuses that mutilated picture of humanity.
God created the astonishing possibility that one human being could look upon another and experience desire so intense that poetry reaches for the language of sickness.
But because God created desire, desire does not become god.
That may be where this gets painfully personal.
Because beautiful things become destructive when we ask them to save us.
Being desired makes a terrible savior.
Another human being makes a terrible savior.
And some of us have discovered that only after bleeding from the attempt.
You thought, If somebody finally chooses me, I will know I matter.
So you accepted attention that should never have been called love.
You ignored warning signs because loneliness was louder.
You stayed because leaving felt like becoming unwanted again.
You confused being pursued with being valued.
You confused sexual attention with intimacy.
You confused somebody needing your body with somebody loving your soul.
Maybe you gave pieces of yourself away because for a few minutes it silenced the terrifying question:
Maybe another message you knew you should not answer.
Another promise that this would be the last time.
Another morning asking God whether grace still reaches people who knew better.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Because Jesus did not come only for people whose desires have always been perfectly ordered.
People with screenshots they hope nobody sees.
People who have slept beside someone and still felt desperately alone.
People who made an idol out of romance.
People who cannot forgive themselves for what happened.
People who have been trying to wash yesterday off their souls for years.
The Gospel does not say your sin was imaginary.
The Gospel says Christ's mercy is greater.
At the cross, Jesus does not redefine darkness as light.
He enters the darkness to rescue sinners from it.
Repentance therefore is not God standing at a distance saying, “Clean yourself before you come closer.”
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who receives sinners.
“Become pure enough so Jesus will want you.”
Jesus Christ came to save sinners, and His grace does not merely pardon us—it begins transforming us.
There is a difference between condemnation and conviction.
“Keep feeding me and eventually I will satisfy you.”
Jesus says, in effect throughout the Gospel:
And perhaps that is why this ancient woman’s confession—I am sick with love—can reach beyond romance and expose something deeper inside all of us.
Always attaching our hearts to something.
“Give me something that will finally quiet this hunger.”
And eventually every created thing reaches the boundary of what it can give.
The lover cannot carry the weight of being God.
The spouse cannot heal every wound.
The sexual experience cannot produce eternal belonging.
And beneath all those smaller hungers remains the terrifyingly beautiful truth:
Human beings were made not merely to consume gifts from God but to know God Himself.
That does not erase human romance.
It puts romance in its proper place.
The Bible can celebrate marital desire precisely because marriage does not have to become salvation.
And the New Testament takes us somewhere breathtaking.
Marriage itself becomes a sign pointing beyond itself.
Paul speaks in Ephesians 5 of husband and wife and then says that this mystery ultimately speaks of Christ and the church.
Not because Jesus is merely a larger version of romantic attraction.
But because covenant love reaches its ultimate redemptive horizon in Christ—the Bridegroom who gives Himself for His people.
At Calvary, Christ demonstrates something infinitely deeper:
That is the difference between lust and cruciform love.
“What can I give for your good?”
Lust reduces a person to appetite.
Love sees a person bearing the image of God.
And Song of Songs, despite all its heat, understands waiting.
“Do not awaken or arouse love until it pleases.”
What a word for an age built upon instant gratification.
We have unprecedented access to bodies and perhaps unprecedented difficulty with intimacy.
We can see strangers naked without knowing their names.
We can simulate closeness without covenant.
We can receive sexual stimulation without sacrifice.
And still, at 2:17 in the morning, the human heart whispers:
Would anybody stay if they knew everything?
That question leads straight toward the scandal of grace.
The parts you edited out of your testimony.
The night you wish you could erase.
The wound somebody else gave you that somehow made you feel dirty even though you were the one harmed.
That does not make sin insignificant.
Christ does not redeem us by pretending rebellion does not matter.
He bears sin and calls sinners to repentance, forgiveness, new life, and holiness.
That means your past does not need to become your permanent address.
There are people reading this who need to hear that sentence again.
Your past does not need to become your permanent address.
You may have awakened love at the wrong time.
You may have awakened desire with the wrong person.
You may have offered your body where there was no covenant.
You may have broken someone else's trust.
You may have built secret habits that are slowly destroying your ability to see another person as a person.
You may have called something love that was actually dependency.
You may have been manipulated by someone who used Scripture itself to control you.
You may have believed that because something happened to your body, your body became permanently ruined.
But Christianity is a resurrection faith.
Jesus specializes in graves people assumed were permanent.
Some relationships should not be restored.
Some phone numbers should remain blocked.
Some patterns need pastoral help, accountability, counseling, and serious intervention.
Grace is not pretending damage never happened.
Grace means damage does not get the final word.
That is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to the same heartbeat:
Not by editing sin until it looks respectable.
By forgiving sinners who repent and making them new.
Maybe your deepest problem today is not sexual sin.
Watched younger people find what you have begged God for.
And somewhere underneath your faithful Christian vocabulary is a sentence you are almost afraid to pray:
Song of Songs gives you permission to acknowledge that longing is physical.
Wanting marriage does not automatically mean Jesus is insufficient.
Wanting affection does not automatically mean you are spiritually immature.
But the ache becomes dangerous when you decide that God must give you another human being before life can have meaning.
No spouse can bear that burden.
No future husband can be Christ.
No future wife can be Christ.
And if God gives you marriage, one of the greatest gifts you can bring into it is refusing to demand that your spouse become your Messiah.
Enjoy the gift without worshiping it.
Because every good human love is still creaturely love.
And maybe you are married, but the fire has dimmed.
You remember when you could hardly stop thinking about each other.
Phones glowing between you in bed.
Two people who once talked until sunrise now scrolling separately in silence.
Song of Songs reminds us that covenant does not require affection to die.
Marriage is more than desire—but it need not become less than tenderness.
Sometimes spiritual maturity looks like praying together.
Sometimes it looks like putting the phone down.
Sometimes it looks like listening again.
Sometimes it looks like remembering that the person beside you is not furniture in your life.
Not as the person who forgot the groceries.
Not merely as the mother or father of your children.
Not merely as the person sharing the mortgage.
The one God entrusted to your love.
And if your marriage contains coercion, violence, or abuse, do not misuse biblical language about covenant as an excuse to conceal danger. Seek wise, trustworthy help and safety.
Biblical love never needs evil to be renamed good.
And perhaps that brings us back to the woman beneath the apple tree.
But Scripture also refuses to let desire become sovereign.
And above every human love stands the God who created us capable of loving at all.
So maybe the question is not whether you desire.
What is your desire teaching you to worship?
That person you cannot stop thinking about…
Have you turned them into salvation?
That relationship you are terrified to lose…
Have you surrendered it to Christ?
Is it training your eyes to consume people instead of love them?
Is it driving you toward Jesus or convincing you to accept anything that temporarily numbs the ache?
Why are you still carrying what Christ is calling you to bring into the light?
This may have hit somewhere you were not expecting.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
But sometimes confession begins when hiding ends.
And if you have spent too long pretending everything is fine:
Someone else reading the comments may discover that they are not the only believer fighting that battle.
Not because every sentence will be needed tonight.
Because there may come a night when one of them will.
You may never know whose midnight your share enters.
Not because anyone must financially support Gospel Warrior in order to glorify God.
Scripture does not give us the right to make that claim.
Biblical giving must never be reduced to spiritual pressure.
But voluntary generosity has always helped Gospel work continue.
Send it privately to somebody who is hurting.
Because the Gospel has never depended upon finding people with spotless histories.
Song of Songs gives us a woman overwhelmed enough to say:
And perhaps tonight you understand that sentence differently.
You know what it is to ache.
But whatever your history, do not make desire your god.
Do not make shame your master.
Do not make another human being your savior.
Bring your desire under the lordship of Christ.
Bring your sexuality under the lordship of Christ.
Bring your loneliness under the lordship of Christ.
Bring your marriage under the lordship of Christ.
Bring your memories under the lordship of Christ.
Bring your body under the lordship of Christ.
Bring the part of the story you thought disqualified you.
Seek help where you are wounded.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Honor what God has made holy.
Because the deepest miracle of grace is not that God finds people who never became messy.
It is that Christ enters the stories we thought were beyond redemption and begins making all things new.
You may still remember the chapter that broke you—but in the hands of Jesus, the chapter that broke you does not get to write the ending.
